OUR FAMILY

1931

TODAY

One of those boys was Jeremy's grandfather. Jill and Jeremy carry it on, raising the same kind of cattle on the same kind of land.

PRICE & PAYING
6
How much does it cost?

Most of our cows weigh 600 to 700 lbs after the butcher cleans them up (called hanging weight). At $8 a pound on the carcass, a half usually runs $2,400 to $2,800, a whole $4,800 to $5,600 and a quarter $1,200 to $1,400. Cutting, wrapping, labeling and freezing are all included. Keep in mind this is an estimate, and your price depends on the weight of your steer.

OUR FAMILY
MEET THE BARTONS

Jill and Jeremy Barton started Barton Beef in 2015. Jeremy's family has raised cattle in Florida for four generations, going all the way back to the 1800s.

JEREMY BARTON
OWNER AND OPERATOR

Jeremy is President of the Flagler County Cattlemen's Association and a retired firefighter and paramedic for the City of Palm Coast. When he isn't working cattle, he's hunting, watching basketball and football, or out on a road trip.

JILL BARTON
OWNER AND OPERATOR

Jill runs communications and finances, so she's the one who answers your email and confirms your order. She loves hot yoga, the lake and the beach, sports, and a good book.

JILL AND JEREMY TODAY
A FAMILY RANCH, STILL HANDS-ON

Jeremy works the cattle. Jill runs the orders, the money and the email, so the person who confirms your order is the same person who raised your beef.

Every cow is born and raised right here in Bunnell, on grass, with hay they bale themselves.

Andrew "Drew" Tucker and Elizabeth "Lizzie" Simmons Tucker.
1800S
FORT CHRISTMAS
DREW AND LIZZIE TUCKER

Jeremy's great-grandparents, Andrew "Drew" and Elizabeth "Lizzie" Tucker, lived in Fort Christmas, Florida. Drew ran about 1,800 head of cattle, sold hides, and farmed citrus and potatoes. Lizzie ran a general store and raised nine sons.

From the Tucker family archive.
1900S
THE TICK YEARS
DIPPING EVERY 14 DAYS

To wipe out cattle fever ticks, the government required ranchers to "dip" their cattle every 14 days, pushing them through a vat of insecticide. For a herd of 1,800, that was hard on the cattle and expensive for the ranch.

ATLANTIC OCEAN
FLAGLER COUNTY
ST. JOHNS RIVER
TICK LINE, NEAR SR 40
FORT CHRISTMAS
START · DREW TUCKER'S HERD
HAW CREEK
NEAR CODY'S CORNER
ABOUT 100 MILES
THREE WEEKS EACH WAY
SKETCH MAP · NOT TO SCALE
1931
THE DRIVE NORTH
TWO BROTHERS, 100 MILES

Drew moved the family and the whole herd just north of the quarantine line, near today's State Road 40, into Flagler County. His son Raymon, 17, and Raymon's brother Gilbert, 14, took a year off school to make two cattle drives from Fort Christmas to Haw Creek near Cody's Corner. Each drive covered about 100 miles over three weeks, including a crossing of the St. Johns River.

There were no fences, so the boys lived in a tent in the woods for seven months to keep the cattle from heading back south. They trapped raccoons, sold the skins and the meat, and used the money to buy a herd of their own.

Working cattle, from the family archive.
1939
40,000 ACRES
DREW'S LAST YEARS

By then Drew owned and leased about 40,000 acres in Flagler and Volusia Counties. He died in 1939 in an accident while working cattle.

The Haw Creek barn: registered Brahman cattle, Santa Gertrudis and quarter horses.
HAW CREEK
RAYMON TUCKER
RAYMON BUILDS THE RANCH

Raymon kept going and built Haw Creek Ranch, putting together several thousand acres in southwest Flagler County. He raised purebred beef cattle, some of the fastest quarter horses in the country, and six daughters. One of them is Denise Tucker Barton, Jeremy's mother. Raymon died in 1998.

The herd today.
2015
BARTON BEEF
PASTURE TO TABLE

Jill and Jeremy started Barton Beef to sell natural, home-raised beef straight to local families, with honest and prompt communication.
